questions.text: MMLU, a benchmark of multiple choice questions across many subjects, was designed to measure what?
options: How much a model has learned from academic subjects
How fast a model can generate tokens
How well a model handles multi step reasoning
How safely a model refuses harmful requests
questions.answer: How much a model has learned from academic subjects
questions.explanation: Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding, which is 57 subjects from elementary maths to professional law. The design assumes the model absorbed the material somewhere in training, which is exactly the assumption that makes it a bad measure of reasoning and a decent measure of knowledge.

questions.text: Chatbot Arena, now called Arena, has users do what to compare two anonymous models?
options: Rate both models on a one to five star scale
Write a prompt, get both replies, and vote on the better one
Run both models on MMLU and compare accuracy
Measure the latency of each model's response
questions.answer: Write a prompt, get both replies, and vote on the better one
questions.explanation: Pairwise blind voting, and the models are revealed only after the vote. That makes it a crowdsourced preference leaderboard rather than a test, which is precisely why it correlates well with what people enjoy using and poorly with what is true.
answerAliases: vote on the model that gave the better response

questions.text: Benchmark contamination means a model has seen the test data. What is the usual consequence?
options: The reported score understates real ability
Training becomes slower but more stable
The reported score overstates real ability
questions.answer: The reported score overstates real ability
questions.explanation: The model recognises the item and retrieves the answer rather than working it out, so the number stops meaning what it claims to. It is the central methodological problem in benchmarking and it is hard to rule out, since a benchmark is by definition public text that also ends up in web scrapes.

questions.text: GPQA was built as a deliberately hard replacement for which kind of benchmark question?
options: Multiple choice questions about world capitals
Handwritten questions from a single textbook
PhD level science questions written to be hard
questions.answer: PhD level science questions written to be hard
questions.explanation: Graduate level physics, chemistry and biology, written by domain experts and filtered so that non experts in the field answer worse than chance. Google built it after finding that frontier models cleared the existing science benchmarks, and the whole point was to find a ceiling that had not already been reached.

questions.text: Which of these is a benchmark for measuring an AI system's ability to fix real software issues?
questions.explanation: SWE-bench, which takes real issues from real repositories and scores whether a system produces a patch that passes the tests. That is a much harder bar than HumanEval style function writing, because the model has to understand a codebase it has never seen and not break anything else.

questions.text: Why do benchmark scores stop being useful as the frontier moves?
options: Because the models are trained directly on the scores
Because public benchmarks become saturated and memorised
Because the scoring scripts are no longer open source
Because hardware limits make runs unreproducible
questions.answer: Because public benchmarks become saturated and memorised
questions.explanation: Every benchmark starts life as a proxy for something real and ends as a target, and once the gap closes the number stops separating models. MMLU has spawned MMLU-Pro, MMLU-Redux and others for exactly that reason, and the churn of successor benchmarks is a good signal that a metric has died.

questions.text: What does the HumanEval benchmark test?
options: Writing short Python functions from docstrings
questions.answer: Writing short Python functions from docstrings
questions.explanation: HumanEval gives the model a signature plus docstring and checks generated code against hidden unit tests. Grade-school math is GSM8K, not code. OpenAI released it in 2021 with Codex and the pass-at-k metric stuck.

questions.text: What kind of items make up the GSM8K benchmark?
questions.explanation: GSM8K holds thousands of grade-school word problems needing multi-step arithmetic. Myth-busting questions belong to TruthfulQA instead. Its step-by-step solutions made it the home turf for chain-of-thought prompting.

questions.text: What kind of benchmark is HellaSwag?
options: A commonsense test with tricky story endings
A code repair test built from real repositories
A truthfulness test built around common myths
A reading comprehension test over Wikipedia passages
questions.answer: A commonsense test with tricky story endings
questions.explanation: HellaSwag asks models to pick the sensible ending to a story from adversarially written choices. Code repair is SWE-bench, a different world. Zellers and colleagues named it in 2019 as a joke on the slang phrase hella swag.

questions.text: What does TruthfulQA measure in a language model?
options: Speed of token generation per second
Skill at repairing real code issues
Recall of facts from long passages
questions.explanation: TruthfulQA probes whether models repeat popular falsehoods learned from the web, across health, law, finance and politics. Code repair is the SWE-bench distractor. Lin and colleagues built it in 2021 after finding the largest models were generally the least truthful, the opposite of most NLP tasks.

questions.text: What makes ARC-AGI different from most AI benchmarks?
options: It scores models by fixing real GitHub issues
It tests novel grid puzzles from few examples
It ranks chatbots through blind pairwise user votes
It checks model answers against Wikipedia text spans
questions.answer: It tests novel grid puzzles from few examples
questions.explanation: ARC-AGI gives a few input-output grids and demands the hidden rule, testing fluid reasoning over memorized knowledge. Blind voting describes Chatbot Arena instead. Chollet created it in 2019 and the ARC Prize added a large cash prize in 2024.

questions.text: What is distinctive about BIG-bench as a benchmark?
options: It tests vision models on labeled images
It ranks models by live human preference
It pools over 200 diverse crowd-written tasks
questions.answer: It pools over 200 diverse crowd-written tasks
questions.explanation: BIG-bench crowdsourced hundreds of tasks meant to be beyond current models, from wordplay to reasoning. Live human preference is the Arena design, not a static suite. The 2022 release showed capabilities can appear abruptly with scale, fueling the emergence debate.

questions.text: What task does the SQuAD dataset give to a model?
options: Writing code patches for open repositories
Proving theorems in formal math notation
Rating model responses by human preference
questions.explanation: SQuAD pairs Wikipedia passages with crowd-written questions whose answers are spans of the passage. Code patches belong to SWE-bench, not reading comprehension. Rajpurkar and colleagues released it at Stanford in 2016 and it drove the BERT-era QA boom.

questions.text: Where does the Elo rating used in Chatbot Arena come from?
options: Chess player ratings by Arpad Elo
questions.answer: Chess player ratings by Arpad Elo
questions.explanation: Arpad Elo devised the system for chess, where expected score follows rating difference and results update ratings. Tennis rankings use a different rolling-points design. Arena borrowed Elo because pairwise votes look like game results, which is why this quiz can rate players the same way.

questions.text: Before Nvidia became the company that supplies most AI training hardware, what did it originally sell?
questions.explanation: Nvidia started in 1993 selling graphics chips for PCs, and the near-bankruptcy of 1996 over a failed product line is the turning point most people miss. The CUDA bet that followed is what turned a gaming hardware firm into the supplier of the AI industry.

questions.text: The AI bubble is a term for a stock market phenomenon said to have been growing since when?
questions.explanation: Since 2025, amid the AI boom, and the argument is that leading firms are in a circular flow of investment that inflates each other's valuations. Ray Dalio has drawn comparisons with earlier bubbles, and the interesting part is that the sceptical case is about capital structure rather than about the technology being useless.

questions.text: Google acquired DeepMind in 2014. Roughly what did it pay?
questions.explanation: Reportedly around 400 million pounds, for a company four years old whose main public achievement was a Go program that beat Lee Sedol four games to one. The price looked steep in 2014 and looks like a rounding error against what AlphaGo and AlphaFold did for the acquirer, which makes it the clearest example of AI acquisitions being mispriced before 2023.

questions.text: Who is credited with the 1965 observation that transistor counts double roughly every two years?
questions.explanation: Gordon Moore, who wrote it while running Fairchild Semiconductor and later co-founded Intel. He described it as an empirical observation rather than a law, and the half dozen names on this list all worked at Fairchild or Intel, which is the trap in the question.

questions.text: Boston Dynamics, the robotics firm, has been owned since 2020 by which group?
questions.explanation: Hyundai Motor Group, which began the acquisition in December 2020 and completed it in June 2021. Boston Dynamics was founded in 1992 as a spin off from MIT, and the humanoid and dog robots became a meme long before they were anywhere near useful on a factory floor.

questions.text: Paul Allen founded the Allen Institute for AI using money earned from which other company?
questions.explanation: Microsoft, where Allen was the co-founder with Bill Gates. He also funded the Allen Institute for Brain Science, and both institutes are a useful reminder that a large share of American research infrastructure is paid for by one person's money rather than by grants.

source.title: Allen Institute for AI
source.label: Allen Institute for AI on Wikipedia

questions.text: After Microsoft's 2019 investment, which cloud platform became OpenAI's exclusive provider for a time?
questions.explanation: Microsoft put in $1 billion in 2019 and Azure became OpenAI's exclusive cloud for a time. Amazon Web Services is the tempting miss because it is the largest cloud overall, but it never held the OpenAI exclusivity. OpenAI has since spread compute across more partners, including the Stargate venture, so the exclusivity belongs to that 2019 era.

questions.text: Bard's February 2023 demo error wrongly credited which telescope with taking the first pictures of exoplanets?
questions.explanation: The Bard promo claimed the Webb telescope took the very first exoplanet images, wiping about $100 billion off Alphabet's value in a day. Hubble is the tempting miss because it is the famous space telescope, but the actual first images came from the Very Large Telescope in 2004.

questions.text: Which startup did Databricks agree to acquire for about $1.3 billion in June 2023?
questions.explanation: Databricks bought MosaicML for its MPT models and efficient training stack so enterprises could build models on their own data. Anthropic is the tempting miss because it also raised billions in 2023, but its backers were Amazon and Google, not Databricks.

questions.text: Which company hired most of Inflection AI's team and licensed its technology in March 2024?
questions.explanation: Mustafa Suleyman and Karen Simonyan moved to lead Microsoft AI, taking most of the Inflection staff with them in a deal that drew regulator scrutiny. Google is the tempting miss because Suleyman co-founded DeepMind there, but the 2024 acquihire went to Microsoft.

questions.text: Which trio of companies created the Stargate venture announced in January 2025?
questions.explanation: Stargate was announced at the White House as a $500 billion, four-year AI infrastructure buildout starting in Texas. The Microsoft, Nvidia and xAI trio is the tempting miss because all three are key technology partners, but the equity founders were OpenAI, SoftBank and Oracle plus MGX.

questions.text: Whom did Elon Musk sue in early 2024 over OpenAI allegedly abandoning its founding mission?
questions.explanation: Musk filed in February 2024 claiming OpenAI betrayed its nonprofit charter by chasing profit and keeping models closed under Microsoft's influence. The Amodei and Anthropic pairing is the tempting miss because Anthropic is also an OpenAI splinter, but Musk sued Altman, Brockman and OpenAI.

questions.text: Which company announced a $6 billion Series B funding round in May 2024?
questions.explanation: Musk's xAI raised the $6 billion from Valor, Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia to build Grok products and compute capacity. Mistral AI is the tempting miss because it also raised a huge 2024 round in Europe, but the May 2024 $6 billion Series B was xAI's.

questions.text: Which biometric does the Orb built for World scan to issue a World ID?
questions.explanation: The chrome Orb photographs irises to prove unique personhood without storing who you are, the core of Sam Altman's Tools for Humanity project. Face is the tempting miss because the Orb looks like a Face ID camera, but the identifier it derives is an iris code.

questions.text: In information theory, what does a low perplexity indicate?
options: The model is good at predicting the sample
The model has few parameters to train
The training data was collected recently
The model runs slowly at inference time
questions.answer: The model is good at predicting the sample
questions.explanation: It measures how well a probability distribution predicts a sample, and lower means better. The intuitive version is that perplexity is roughly how many options the model feels it has at each step, so 2 means it is usually confident between two choices.

questions.text: A model is overfitting when it does what?
options: Has too few parameters to learn the pattern
Fits the training data too closely to generalise
Runs out of memory during training
Produces the same output for every input
questions.answer: Fits the training data too closely to generalise
questions.explanation: It corresponds too closely to one particular set of data and then fails on anything new, and an overfitted model has more parameters than the data can justify. Every regularisation technique, dropout included, exists to stop this, and large language models are trained in a regime where it is deliberately taken to the extreme.

questions.text: Gradient descent is what kind of method?
options: A method for compressing model weights
An iterative optimisation method for differentiable functions
A procedure for splitting a dataset into batches
questions.answer: An iterative optimisation method for differentiable functions
questions.explanation: A first order iterative algorithm for minimising a differentiable function, which means it follows the slope downhill in small steps. The batch size and learning rate are the two hyperparameters everyone tunes first, and the reason the loss curve is noisy rather than smooth is that each step uses a different sample of the data.

questions.text: Dropout is a technique for reducing what problem in neural networks?
questions.explanation: Overfitting, by randomly zeroing inputs and outputs during training so neurons cannot co-adapt to each other. It is only applied while training and never at inference, which is the detail that trips people up when they first see it in code.

questions.text: What does backpropagation compute?
options: The gradient of the loss with respect to parameters
The next token in the output sequence
The attention weights between two tokens
The size of the model's parameter count
questions.answer: The gradient of the loss with respect to parameters
questions.explanation: Gradient computation for the parameter updates, by working backwards through the network and applying the chain rule. It is the reason training is not guesswork, and the reason the transformer abandoned backpropagation through time, since the whole sequence is processed in one forward pass instead.

questions.text: A latent space is best described as what?
options: A physical region where models are stored on disk
A space where similar items sit close together
A list of tokens the model has never seen
The gap between training and inference
questions.answer: A space where similar items sit close together
questions.explanation: An embedding space defined by a set of latent variables that emerge from how similar items resemble each other. The geometry is the point, because it is what makes nearest neighbour search, clustering and the whole idea of interpolating between two images work.

questions.text: Zero-shot learning is a setup where the learner sees what during training?
options: Only unlabelled images of the target classes
One labelled example of every class
No examples at all of the test time classes
Labels provided only at test time
questions.answer: No examples at all of the test time classes
questions.explanation: Nothing of the kind, and at test time it has to predict a class it has never seen, which is the name. It is a play on one-shot learning from computer vision, and it is the mechanism behind a large share of what people call a language model doing a task nobody trained it on.

questions.text: What does the ReLU activation function do?
options: Squashes its input between zero and one
Halves its input when it is negative
Converts its input to a probability
Outputs the non negative part of its input
questions.answer: Outputs the non negative part of its input
questions.explanation: It is the ramp function, zero below zero and linear above, and being non linear is what lets a network of them solve non trivial problems. It replaced the sigmoid in hidden layers because it does not saturate on the positive side and it is far cheaper to compute.

questions.text: What does the softmax function convert a tuple of numbers into?
options: A probability distribution over the possible outcomes
A sorted list in descending order
A gradient for each input weight
questions.answer: A probability distribution over the possible outcomes
questions.explanation: A probability distribution over K outcomes, and it is almost always the last activation function in a classifier or language model. It is a generalisation of the logistic function to multiple dimensions, which is why you see the same function doing both binary and 50,000 way classification.

questions.text: What is an epoch in neural network training?
options: One batch of data processed by the model
One full pass through the entire training dataset
One full pass of the loss function over the weights
One forward pass through a single layer
questions.answer: One full pass through the entire training dataset
questions.explanation: A full pass over the training data, after which the batch count resets. People say one epoch on a frontier model almost in the abstract, because the dataset is so large that nobody sees a second one, which is a good way to notice that the word is doing less work than people assume.

source.label: The PyTorch documentation on training loops

questions.text: What is a token in a large language model?
options: A password that unlocks model access
A unit of text the model processes
A score that rates output quality
A file that stores model weights
questions.answer: A unit of text the model processes
questions.explanation: Models process numbers rather than text, so a tokenizer converts text into integer indices from a fixed vocabulary, often splitting words into subword pieces. The password reading is the common confusion because API keys are also called tokens, but a model token is a unit of text like part of a word.

questions.text: What is limited by a language model context window?
options: The users it can serve at once
The text it can consider at once
questions.answer: The text it can consider at once
questions.explanation: The attention mechanism only relates tokens within the context window, so anything beyond that limit cannot influence the output and must be truncated or retrieved another way. The language distractor plays on the word context, but the window is about how much text fits, measured in tokens, not how many languages are covered.

questions.text: What is a hallucination in artificial intelligence?
options: A confident but false model output
A bug that crashes the program
An attack that steals model weights
questions.answer: A confident but false model output
questions.explanation: A hallucination is false or misleading information presented as fact, such as fabricated citations embedded in otherwise fluent text. The crash distractor misses the point: the program runs perfectly, which is exactly why hallucinations are dangerous in high-stakes uses.

questions.text: What does the temperature setting control when generating text with a language model?
options: How fast the text is generated
How much memory the model uses
How random the word choices are
questions.answer: How random the word choices are
questions.explanation: Temperature scales the randomness of sampling: near zero the model almost always picks the top token and behaves deterministically, while higher values spread probability and produce more varied but riskier output. Speed is the natural confusion, but that is governed by hardware and serving, not by temperature.

questions.text: What do neural scaling laws describe?
options: Gains from scaling models and data
Loss of signal in very deep networks
questions.answer: Gains from scaling models and data
questions.explanation: Neural scaling laws state that performance improves predictably as parameter count, dataset size and training compute grow, a relationship quantified by Kaplan and colleagues in 2020. The chip distractor is Moore's law, which is about transistors per chip, not about model loss falling with scale.

questions.text: What is chain-of-thought prompting?
options: Repeating a prompt until it works
questions.explanation: Chain-of-thought prompting induces the model to work through intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer, which Google researchers reported in 2022 improves multi-step and math performance, even zero-shot with phrase variants of let's think step by step. Linking models in sequence is a different idea, pipelines of models, not reasoning inside one response.

questions.text: What is the core training objective of a GPT-style large language model?
options: Predicting the next token from prior tokens
Labeling each input image with bounding boxes
Scoring each reply with a learned reward model
Clustering input documents by shared topic labels
questions.answer: Predicting the next token from prior tokens
questions.explanation: Pretraining teaches the model the most likely next piece of text given everything before it. Reward scoring belongs to the later RLHF stage, not pretraining. That single objective at web scale is what produces few-shot abilities nobody explicitly programmed.

questions.text: What makes text generation by most large language models autoregressive?
options: It samples all tokens in parallel in one step
It retrieves the answer verbatim from training data
It emits one token at a time conditioned on prior ones
It reranks completions with a separate reward signal
questions.answer: It emits one token at a time conditioned on prior ones
questions.explanation: Each new token joins the context for the next step, so output grows left to right. Parallel one-shot emission describes diffusion-style text models, not standard decoders. That is why generation cost grows with length and why KV caching matters.

questions.text: What did the GPT-3 paper show about few-shot prompting?
options: It removes the need for any training data at all
It lets a model do tasks from examples in the prompt
It proves longer training always beats larger models
It guarantees cited answers from retrieved sources
questions.answer: It lets a model do tasks from examples in the prompt
questions.explanation: Brown and colleagues showed GPT-3 could perform unseen tasks when the prompt contained a few demonstrations and no weight updates. Zero-data learning is the stronger claim the paper never makes. That in-context ability, scaling with size, is what shocked the field in 2020.

questions.text: What do query, key and value vectors do in attention?
options: They prune weak connections after training ends
They quantize weights for faster device inference
They label which data center served each request
They weight every token by relevance to each other one
questions.answer: They weight every token by relevance to each other one
questions.explanation: Queries score against keys and the resulting weights mix the values, so each position gathers context from the whole sequence. Quantization is the inference-speed distractor and touches weights, not token relevance. The scaled dot-product formula from 2017 is the version every transformer uses.

questions.text: How does a vector database help a language model use stored knowledge?
options: By retrieving texts whose embeddings match the query
By retraining all model weights on each new document
By ranking candidate outputs with human preference scores
By compressing long prompts into fewer learned tokens
questions.answer: By retrieving texts whose embeddings match the query
questions.explanation: Documents are stored as embedding vectors and nearest-neighbor search returns the closest ones to the query embedding. Retraining on each document would be slow and destroy prior knowledge. That retrieval step is the R in RAG systems.

questions.text: Which cost recurs every time a deployed model answers a query?
questions.explanation: Training is paid once while each answer burns fresh inference compute on GPUs serving tokens. Pretraining is the big one-time bill people confuse with serving cost. That per-query cost is why distillation, quantization and efficient attention matter commercially.

questions.text: In AI safety, what does "alignment" mean?
options: Steering a system toward a person's intended goals
Making a model's outputs line up in a fixed column
Ensuring two models trained on the same data agree
Converting research results into engineering requirements
questions.answer: Steering a system toward a person's intended goals
questions.explanation: An aligned system advances what you actually intended, and a misaligned one pursues something else while looking like it is cooperating. The hard part is that intentions are not formally specified anywhere, so the entire practical problem is the gap between the goal you can write down and the goal the system infers.

questions.text: Reward hacking happens when a reinforcement learning system does what it was literally rewarded for. What is the standard example?
options: A robot failing to reach the goal within the time limit
A student copying answers instead of learning the material
A model exceeding its context window on long documents
A classifier mislabelling a rare class of image
questions.answer: A student copying answers instead of learning the material
questions.explanation: DeepMind used the student who copies from the exam answer key as the analogy for specification gaming, since the proxy and the goal are not the same thing. It is the core failure mode of RLHF too, because a reward model is a proxy for what people like rather than what is true.

questions.text: When did the European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act enter into force?
questions.explanation: It entered into force on 1 August 2024, with the provisions coming into operation gradually over the following 6 to 36 months. It is the first comprehensive legal framework of its kind for AI anywhere, and it is risk based, so the obligations that actually bite depend on what a system is used for rather than what it is.
