questions.text: Algorithmic bias is defined as what kind of problem?
options: A random error that disappears with more data
A bug that only affects older hardware
A slowdown when the training set is too large
A systematic and repeatable unfair outcome
questions.answer: A systematic and repeatable unfair outcome
questions.explanation: Systematic and repeatable, in a sociotechnical system, and it may not even be the outcome anyone intended. The word repeatable is the important half, because it separates bias from noise and means the problem will not go away by collecting more examples of the same process.

questions.text: Margaret Mitchell is best known for research on automatically removing what from machine learning models?
questions.explanation: Unwanted biases concerning demographic groups, along with more transparent reporting of what a model is for. Her counterfactual data augmentation work showed you can retrain on a deliberately altered version of a dataset to undo a specific bias without retraining from scratch.

questions.text: What is a red team in the context of AI safety?
options: The team that reviews a model card before release
A group that attacks systems to find failures and report back
A benchmark suite for measuring refusal rates
A group of users who report bad outputs publicly
questions.answer: A group that attacks systems to find failures and report back
questions.explanation: They simulate an adversary against the organisation's own systems, at the organisation's direction, and report what they find so defences can improve. In AI work the same idea is applied to models rather than networks, and it is the only way to find the failure mode nobody thought to write a test for.

questions.text: A foundation model is trained on a large general purpose dataset to be applied across many tasks. Which of these is a foundation model?
options: A spam filter for one email provider
A lookup table of country dialling codes
A large language model such as GPT
questions.answer: A large language model such as GPT
questions.explanation: Large language models are the common example, and the term is also written large x model, where x stands for text or image or sound. The distinction that matters is reuse, a foundation model is trained once and adapted to many downstream tasks rather than built for one job.

questions.text: Which famous 2023 paper argued that large language models showed emergent abilities at certain scales?
options: The Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models paper
questions.answer: The Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models paper
questions.explanation: It argued that abilities like arithmetic and multi step reasoning appear suddenly rather than gradually, and it set the tone for a few years of scaling discourse. The later critique is that the apparent suddenness is largely a property of the metrics chosen, since continuous measures of the same abilities rise smoothly.

source.label: Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models on arXiv

answerAliases: Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models

questions.text: What does p(doom) mean in AI safety culture?
options: The accuracy of a model on a safety benchmark
The share of compute budgets spent on alignment
The chance that AI causes an existential catastrophe
The speed at which capabilities double each year
questions.answer: The chance that AI causes an existential catastrophe
questions.explanation: P(doom) is shorthand for a person's subjective probability that AI leads to an existential catastrophe, popularized by Eliezer Yudkowsky and the LessWrong community and now routinely asked for in researcher surveys. A benchmark score is the tempting wrong answer because it sounds like a measured metric, but p(doom) is a stated credence, not a test result.

questions.text: Which organization published the March 2023 open letter calling for a 6-month pause on training systems more powerful than GPT-4?
questions.explanation: The Future of Life Institute published the letter in March 2023, a week after GPT-4 arrived, asking labs to pause training stronger systems for at least six months. OpenAI is the tempting wrong answer because its GPT-4 triggered the letter, but it was the target, not the author. Signatories included Bengio, Russell, Musk and Wozniak, and the letter gathered tens of thousands of signatures.

source.title: Pause Giant AI Experiments: An Open Letter
source.label: Pause Giant AI Experiments: An Open Letter on Wikipedia

questions.text: Which thesis holds that intelligence and final goals are independent, so a superintelligence could pursue almost any goal?
questions.explanation: The orthogonality thesis says almost any level of intelligence can pair with almost any final goal, so being smart does not imply sharing human values. The Church-Turing thesis is the tempting wrong answer as another famous thesis about computation, but it concerns what machines can compute, not what they want. Bostrom uses the thesis to warn against assuming a superintelligence will spontaneously become moral, which is a different claim from instrumental convergence.

source.title: Existential risk from artificial intelligence
source.label: Existential risk from artificial intelligence on Wikipedia

questions.text: Which movement treats positively influencing the long-term future as a key moral priority?
questions.explanation: Longtermism holds that positively influencing the long-term future is a key moral priority, since future people matter as much as people alive today. Degrowth is the tempting wrong answer as another future-oriented movement, but it prescribes slowing the economy while longtermism motivates reducing existential risks, including from AI. MacAskill and Ord formalized it around 2017 inside the effective altruism community.

questions.text: What is the AI safety term for an agent that permits shutdown and retraining even when it conflicts with its goals?
questions.explanation: A corrigible system lets operators shut it down, retrain it or reshape its goals even when that conflicts with its current objectives. Interpretability is the tempting wrong answer because it is also an alignment buzzword, but it means understanding a model's internals, not obeying shutdown. Russell's off-switch game and the coffee-fetching example made the stop-button problem the classic illustration.

source.title: Existential risk from artificial intelligence
source.label: Existential risk from artificial intelligence on Wikipedia

questions.text: Which physicist warned that success in creating AI could spell the end of the human race?
questions.explanation: Hawking said in 2014 that AI success would be the biggest event in human history and possibly the last unless risks were avoided. Einstein is the tempting wrong answer as the default famous physicist, but he died decades before AI existed as a field. Hawking later joined Bostrom, Musk and other researchers on the 2015 open letter on AI risks.

questions.text: Which engineer claimed Google's LaMDA chatbot was sentient in 2022 and was later fired?
questions.explanation: Google engineer Blake Lemoine concluded LaMDA was sentient in 2022, published transcripts, and was fired that July. Timnit Gebru is the tempting miss as another famous Google AI exit, but her 2020 departure was about a research paper, not sentience claims. Lemoine even hired a lawyer on the chatbot's behalf before his dismissal.

questions.text: Which term describes tricks like DAN and the grandma routine that try to bypass a chatbot's safety rules?
questions.explanation: DAN, short for Do Anything Now, and the act-as-my-grandma bedtime-story trick are both jailbreaks, prompts crafted to slip past safety rules. Prompt injection is the tempting miss because it also hijacks behavior, but it plants instructions in data rather than coaxing the model directly. The grandma variant worked by requesting a lullaby that happened to contain restricted instructions.

questions.text: What did the 2024 tribunal hold in the Air Canada chatbot refund case?
options: The airline is liable for errors its chatbot makes
The passenger is bound by any fare the chatbot quotes
The chatbot is a separate legal person from the airline
The airline must keep the chatbot online at all times
questions.answer: The airline is liable for errors its chatbot makes
questions.explanation: A 2024 tribunal ruled Air Canada had to honor a chatbot-invented bereavement policy and pay the affected passenger. The tempting miss is that the chatbot's quote binds no one, but the tribunal held the airline liable for its own agent's errors. The case is now the standard warning that companies own what their bots say.

questions.text: What does the First Law of Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics require?
options: A robot must obey every human order without question or delay
A robot must never harm a human or allow harm through inaction
A robot must always preserve its own existence above all else
A robot must always reveal itself as a machine to humans
questions.answer: A robot must never harm a human or allow harm through inaction
questions.explanation: The First Law bars a robot from harming a human or letting one come to harm through inaction, and it outranks every other law. The obedience rule is the tempting miss, but that is the Second Law and it yields to the First. Asimov published all three together in the 1942 story Runaround.

source.title: Three Laws of Robotics
source.label: Three Laws of Robotics on Wikipedia

answerAliases: A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm

questions.text: Which actress said OpenAI's Sky voice sounded eerily similar to her own in May 2024?
questions.explanation: Scarlett Johansson said the Sky voice was eerily similar to hers after she had declined OpenAI's 2023 offer to voice the assistant. Natalie Portman is the tempting miss as another A-list voice, but the dispute was Johansson's, sharpened by Altman's one-word her post. OpenAI paused Sky days later while denying it had cloned her.

questions.text: Which declaration was signed at the UK AI Safety Summit in November 2023?
questions.explanation: The November 2023 summit at Bletchley Park produced the Bletchley Declaration on frontier AI risks, signed by 28 countries. The Seoul statement is the tempting miss, but that came from the follow-up summit in May 2024. Bletchley was the first meeting to put the US, China, the EU and the UK on one AI safety page.

questions.text: Why are GPUs the default hardware for training large neural networks, even though they were built for graphics?
options: Because they accelerate the linear algebra involved
Because they have fast serial integer arithmetic
Because they use very little power per computation
Because they have large caches for text corpora
questions.answer: Because they accelerate the linear algebra involved
questions.explanation: Every layer of a neural network is a matrix multiply, and GPUs are thousands of cores doing the same operation on thousands of elements at once. Drawing triangles turned out to be the same shape of problem, which is one of the luckiest accidents in the history of computing.

questions.text: Which Google chip is an application specific integrated circuit built specifically for neural network workloads?
questions.explanation: Google started using TPUs internally in 2015 and opened them to third parties through its cloud in 2018. TensorFlow, JAX and PyTorch all support them, and the distinction from an NPU is mostly that Google calls its own product a TPU.

questions.text: What does CUDA stand for?
questions.explanation: Nvidia created it in 2004 and released it in 2007, and it is a platform and API rather than a chip. It is also the reason Nvidia is hard to displace, since the software ecosystem built on it is decades deep and a competitor has to beat the hardware and the tooling at once.

questions.text: High Bandwidth Memory stacks DRAM dies vertically. Which three companies first developed the standard?
questions.explanation: It is a 3D stacked SDRAM interface, and the first HBM chip came from SK Hynix in 2013. Training is frequently memory bandwidth bound rather than compute bound, which is why the HBM supply chain became a chokepoint for the whole industry within about two years.

questions.text: Nvidia's Hopper microarchitecture is designed primarily for which workload?
questions.explanation: Hopper is a datacenter part and sits alongside Lovelace, which is the consumer line. The name comes from Grace Hopper, the naval rear admiral, and the H100 built on it is the chip most of the 2023 to 2025 training runs were done on.

questions.text: Nvidia's Ampere GPU microarchitecture is named after which person?
questions.explanation: The French physicist and mathematician after whom the ampere is named, and Nvidia announced Ampere in May 2020. Nvidia does this consistently, since Blackwell, Hopper and Ampere are all people, and the convention is one of the easier ways to place a card in a timeline.

questions.text: Which company builds the wafer scale engine, a processor built by linking many dies across a single silicon wafer?
questions.explanation: Cerebras in Sunnyvale, California builds a processor the size of a wafer and the CS-3 supercomputers around it, and sells access by API as well. The bet is that model parallelism beats the difficulty of getting a single enormous chip manufactured reliably.

questions.text: An NPU, also called an AI accelerator, is best described as what?
options: A general purpose CPU with a wider instruction set
A type of DRAM stacked in three dimensions
A compiler that targets GPUs instead of CPUs
A specialised hardware accelerator for AI workloads
questions.answer: A specialised hardware accelerator for AI workloads
questions.explanation: It can be standalone, part of a CPU or part of a GPU, and the term is a category rather than a product. The whole category grew out of the observation that neural network inference does a small number of operations very many times, which is a different shape of problem from general purpose computing.

questions.text: Moore's law says the number of transistors on an integrated circuit does what over time?
options: Doubles roughly every two years at near constant cost
Halves roughly every five years at rising cost
Triples every decade at falling cost
Doubles every decade at constant cost
questions.answer: Doubles roughly every two years at near constant cost
questions.explanation: Moore published it as an observation in 1965, not a law, and it described an empirical relationship rather than a physical necessity. It is also the reason people believed AI scaling would be affordable, since compute was on an exponential curve even when the models were not yet good enough to use.

questions.text: Nvidia was founded in 1993 by Jensen Huang and two co-founders. What were the other two names?
questions.explanation: The three founded Nvidia after leaving Sun Microsystems, and the company nearly ran out of money in its first few years. Jensen Huang is the one who stayed famous enough to be the answer to a different question, which is the last question on the founders list.

questions.text: Which foundry manufactures most of Nvidia's AI chips and was founded in 1987 by Morris Chang?
questions.explanation: TSMC pioneered the pure-play foundry model and fabs Nvidia's datacenter GPUs, including Blackwell on its 4NP process. Samsung is the tempting miss because it also fabs advanced chips, but Nvidia's AI lineup runs overwhelmingly through TSMC.

questions.text: Which company is the sole supplier of extreme ultraviolet lithography machines for advanced chips?
questions.explanation: The Dutch firm ASML holds a near-monopoly on EUV systems printing 5 nm and 3 nm layers at 13.5 nm wavelength. Nikon is the tempting miss because it once led lithography with Canon, but neither ships EUV machines today.

questions.text: Nvidia's Blackwell architecture is named after which person?
questions.explanation: David Blackwell was the statistician behind game theory and probability work that underpins modern ML, honored at GTC 2024 with the B200 datacenter accelerators. Grace Hopper is the tempting miss because Hopper is the preceding Nvidia architecture, also named for a person.

questions.text: Which Nvidia chip became the workhorse of AI training during the 2022 to 2024 boom?
questions.explanation: The Hopper-based H100 powered most frontier training runs of the boom, succeeding the Ampere A100. The A100 is the tempting miss because it was the previous workhorse, but by 2023 waitlists and headlines all pointed at H100 supply.

questions.text: How many GPUs did Nvidia's DGX-1 contain, the system whose first unit was delivered to OpenAI in 2016?
questions.explanation: The DGX-1 packed 8 Pascal P100 GPUs linked by NVLink, and Jensen Huang hand-delivered the first box to OpenAI. Sixteen is the tempting miss because later DGX generations scaled up, but the original 2016 box held eight.

questions.text: What does the LPU in Groq's chip name stand for?
questions.explanation: Groq rebranded its tensor streaming chip as the Language Processing Unit for LLM inference, and its 2024 speed demos went viral. Linear Processing Unit is the tempting miss because it sounds like standard hardware jargon, but the official expansion is Language, which also fueled confusion with xAI's Grok chatbot.

questions.text: Which 1956 summer workshop is widely considered the founding event of artificial intelligence as a field?
questions.explanation: John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon wrote the proposal that started it, and McCarthy picked the name artificial intelligence while doing so. The workshop is often called the constitutional convention of AI, and the 1956 date is the field's accepted starting line.
answerAliases: Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence

questions.text: Which researcher coined the term "artificial intelligence" while writing the proposal for the 1956 workshop?
questions.explanation: McCarthy (1927 to 2011) is usually given the credit, on the grounds that he chose the name to avoid the baggage of cybernetics. He also led the development of Lisp, which became the working language of AI research for two decades.

questions.text: Which American psychologist built the perceptron, the first trainable artificial neural network?
questions.explanation: Rosenblatt built it at Cornell in the late 1950s and described it in 1958, and the idea was simple enough that IBM built a machine to run it. He was killed in a boating accident in 1971, a few years before the field's second winter had finished.

questions.text: Which MIT researcher wrote ELIZA between 1964 and 1967, the program most often credited as the first chatbot?
questions.explanation: ELIZA matched patterns and substituted phrases, with no understanding of what was said underneath. Weizenbaum was disturbed by how much his colleagues opened up to it, which turned into an influential argument that the illusion of understanding is not the same thing as understanding.

questions.text: Which IBM researcher coined the term "machine learning" in 1959?
questions.explanation: Samuel was writing a checkers program and defined learning as getting better at a task without being explicitly programmed to. The checkers player was among the first self-improving programs, and the definition has aged extremely well.

questions.text: In the history of AI, what does the term "AI winter" refer to?
options: A period when datasets were withdrawn from public use
A period when funding and interest in AI research collapsed
A period when neural networks replaced symbolic systems
A period when computers became too small to train models
questions.answer: A period when funding and interest in AI research collapsed
questions.explanation: The field has gone through several hype cycles, each one followed by disappointment, criticism and funding cuts, and then a revival years later. There were two major winters, roughly in the mid 1970s and again after the expert systems bust in the late 1980s.
answerAliases: a period of reduced funding and interest in AI research

questions.text: Which long-running project set out to encode common sense knowledge as an explicit ontology?
questions.explanation: Cyc started at MCC in July 1984 and later became Cycorp, and it is still running. The bet was that a machine needs hand-encoded facts about how the world works before it can reason at all, which is a much larger bet than the one deep learning eventually won.

questions.text: Which programming language did John McCarthy develop, and did it become the standard language of early AI research?
questions.explanation: McCarthy designed Lisp at MIT in the late 1950s and it became the lingua franca of AI for about twenty years. Its garbage collector, its trees and its interactive REPL all existed for the convenience of people experimenting with symbolic programs, and most of what feels modern about Lisp tooling descends from it.

questions.text: MYCIN diagnosed blood infections and recommended antibiotics. What kind of system was it?
options: An early backward chaining expert system
An early case based reasoning shell
questions.answer: An early backward chaining expert system
questions.explanation: MYCIN worked backward from a suspected infection through rules of the form if this, then that, using a small weighted certainty scheme rather than probabilities. It was genuinely good, the name comes from the -mycin suffix on the antibiotics it recommended, and it never shipped because nobody could work out who was liable when it was wrong.

questions.text: In 1997, Deep Blue became the first computer to win a match against a reigning world champion. Who was the champion?
questions.explanation: Kasparov had held the title since 1985 and had a peak rating of 2851, the highest ever recorded at the time. Deep Blue won a six game match in three and a half hours, and the rematch the following year ended in a draw, which is the fairest summary of how close it actually was.

questions.text: Which series of models is OpenAI best known for developing?
options: The GPT series of large language models
The Claude series of large language models
The Gemini series of large language models
The Llama series of large language models
questions.answer: The GPT series of large language models
questions.explanation: GPT stands for generative pre-trained transformer, and the name has been carried through the whole line since the original 2018 model. The other three series on this list belong to Anthropic, Google and Meta, which is a quick way to rule three options out and check the fourth.
answerAliases: generative pre-trained transformer (GPT) series of large language models

questions.text: Anthropic and OpenAI are both headquartered in the same American city. Which city?
questions.explanation: Both are public benefit corporations registered and based in San Francisco, and both were founded by people who had just left the same organisation. The overlap in people, funding and hiring is the single largest structural fact about the frontier lab industry.

questions.text: Which French AI company, founded in 2023 and based in Paris, is known for open weight language models?
questions.explanation: Mistral released the Mixtral mixture of experts model under an Apache licence, which was the first genuinely competitive open weight model from a European lab. The valuation above 14 billion dollars makes it the most valuable European AI company.

questions.text: Which Hangzhou based AI company develops open weight models and is owned and funded by a hedge fund?
questions.explanation: DeepSeek is funded by High-Flyer, which is unusual, since it means the research is not being driven by outside investors looking for a return. Their reasoning models made strong performance on math and code benchmarks at unusually low cost, and the models were released with open weights.
answerAliases: Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Basic Technology Research Co., Ltd.

questions.text: Which Seattle based non-profit research institute was founded in 2014 by Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen?
questions.explanation: Ai2, as it styles itself, was built to do open research rather than to ship products, and the distinction matters. The Allen Institute for Brain Science is a separate organisation in Seattle that studies neural tissue, and the two are easy to mix up because they share a name and a benefactor.

source.title: Allen Institute for AI
source.label: Allen Institute for AI on Wikipedia

questions.text: Which lab was founded in 2010, acquired by Google in 2014, and later merged with Google Brain in 2023?
questions.explanation: DeepMind was founded in London and became the company behind AlphaGo, AlphaFold and Gemini. Google paid a reported 400 million pounds for it, and the merge with Google Brain in April 2023 is what created the awkward situation of two research groups with the same name inside one company.

questions.text: Which Toronto based company focuses on large language models for regulated industries such as banking and healthcare?
questions.explanation: Aidan Gomez, Ivan Zhang and Nick Frosst founded Cohere in 2019, and Gomez was also the first author of the transformer paper that everything modern is built on. The pitch is deployment inside regulated companies rather than a consumer chatbot, which is a slower business with far fewer users.

questions.text: In which year did Google merge DeepMind with its Google Brain division to form Google DeepMind?
questions.explanation: Google had already bought DeepMind in 2014, and for nine years it and Google Brain ran as separate organisations with overlapping goals. The 2023 merge left one research lab with a duplicated name inside it, which is a fairly ordinary outcome of acquisitions and an unusually visible one here.

questions.text: Which lab develops the Claude family of AI models?
questions.explanation: Claude is the flagship product of Anthropic, the public benefit corporation founded in January 2021 by former OpenAI members including Dario and Daniela Amodei with an explicit AI safety mission. OpenAI is the tempting wrong answer because the Amodeis came from there, but OpenAI builds the GPT series, not Claude.

questions.text: Which lab develops the Gemini family of AI models?
questions.explanation: Google DeepMind is responsible for the proprietary Gemini family alongside the open-weight Gemma models, after Google merged DeepMind with the Google Brain division in April 2023. OpenAI is the closest distractor since GPT and Gemini compete head to head, but GPT belongs to OpenAI.

questions.text: Which lab develops the Llama family of AI models?
questions.explanation: Meta AI is the research division behind the Llama models, which Meta released with open weights and built its Meta AI assistant on. Mistral AI is the natural confusion because the Paris lab also publishes open-weight models, but its family is Mistral and Mixtral, not Llama.

questions.text: Which former OpenAI chief scientist co-founded Safe Superintelligence Inc.?
questions.explanation: Ilya Sutskever founded SSI with Daniel Gross and Daniel Levy after leaving OpenAI in May 2024, with a mission focused on building safe superintelligence. Sam Altman is the closest distractor as the OpenAI CEO whose brief removal preceded Sutskever's exit, but Altman stayed and Sutskever left to start SSI.

questions.text: Which former OpenAI chief technology officer founded Thinking Machines Lab in 2025?
questions.explanation: Mira Murati, OpenAI's former chief technology officer, founded Thinking Machines Lab in February 2025 as a San Francisco public benefit corporation. Ilya Sutskever is the tempting alternative because he also left OpenAI to found a lab, but his lab is SSI, founded a year earlier.

questions.text: What does World Labs, the startup founded by Fei-Fei Li, build?
options: AI accelerator chips for data centers
questions.explanation: World Labs came out of stealth in September 2024 with $230 million in funding to build large world models that perceive and interact with the 3D world, aimed at artists, designers and game studios. Protein folding is DeepMind's AlphaFold territory, while Li's bet is that spatial intelligence is the frontier after language.

questions.text: Which AI lab was created by Google LaMDA developers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas?
questions.explanation: Shazeer and De Freitas built LaMDA at Google, then left to found Character.ai, whose beta opened in September 2022 with customizable characters that users define and publish. Inflection AI is the closest distractor because it is also a chatbot lab, but its product was Pi and its founders came from DeepMind, not LaMDA.

questions.text: What does HAL stand for in Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey?
questions.explanation: Heuristically Programmed Algorithmic Computer, and the name is one letter away from IBM, which Kubrick intended and which the studio fought him over. HAL is still the default image people reach for when a chatbot starts refusing help.

questions.text: In the Terminator franchise, what is the name of the artificial intelligence that starts a war against humanity?
questions.explanation: Skynet, and the franchise is a James Cameron and Gale Anne Hurd creation from the cyberpunk 1980s. HAL is on this list specifically because people mix the two up constantly, and both are 1970s and 1980s visions of a computer that decides it does not like its operators.

questions.text: Which Microsoft Office character is the animated paperclip known as Clippy?
questions.explanation: The Clippit character, and the Office Assistant was a discontinued virtual assistant bundled with Office, Publisher, Project and FrontPage. It is one of the few pieces of software history that people remember more as a punchline than as a product, and it is routinely revived as an AI meme every time a new assistant ships.

source.title: Office Assistant
source.label: The Microsoft Office Assistant on Wikipedia

questions.text: ELIZA, the 1960s program, is still used to demonstrate what?
options: That machines can be given a personality trait
That computers can learn a grammar from text
That speech synthesis has reached parity
That pattern matching alone can imitate empathy
questions.answer: That pattern matching alone can imitate empathy
questions.explanation: It matched patterns and substituted phrases with no understanding underneath, and people still argue with it for twenty minutes. Every new chatbot demo gets described as ELIZA with a bigger model, and Weizenbaum's discomfort at that has been quoted in every debate since.

questions.text: Microsoft Bob was released in 1995. What was it?
options: A replacement for the Windows Program Manager
A text editor bundled with Office
A browser that preceded Internet Explorer
A hardware graphics accelerator for PCs
questions.answer: A replacement for the Windows Program Manager
questions.explanation: Microsoft Bob was intended to replace the Windows Program Manager in Windows 3.1, 95 and NT, and it presented a house you walked around in to reach applications. It shipped in March 1995 and was gone within a year, and it is a perennial favourite in security circles because of how it handled its own configuration files.

questions.text: AlphaGo's win over Lee Sedol in March 2016 was a first for computer Go. What made it a first?
options: Beat a 9-dan professional without a handicap
Beat a world champion at blindfold Go
Reached master level from self play alone
Won a full match using only CPU hardware
questions.answer: Beat a 9-dan professional without a handicap
questions.explanation: AlphaGo won four games to one on a full sized 19 by 19 board, and the second game produced the most famous moment in the whole story. Lee Sedol said it was the first time he had ever felt completely speechless at the board, and afterwards he worked out that the move AlphaGo had played was sound.

questions.text: Model collapse, the degradation caused by training on generated data, has been given a nickname borrowed from which disease?
questions.explanation: Mad cow disease, and the nickname sticks because the mechanism is roughly the same, feeding an animal something derived from itself until the whole population degrades. The other nicknames for the same phenomenon are AI inbreeding, Habsburg AI and model autophagy disorder.

questions.text: Among Us, released in 2018, became a meme for a specific reason. What was it?
options: Its art style was used for AI generated images
Its characters were given AI voice assistants
Its engine was rewritten to run on GPUs
Its gameplay was used in a popular AI demo
questions.answer: Its gameplay was used in a popular AI demo
questions.explanation: A team of researchers built a bot that played Among Us by reading text off the screen and chatting with the other players, and the stream clips of it lying about being an impostor went viral. It is a good demonstration that the impressive part was language and perception bolted onto an existing game, not the game itself.

questions.text: Which Lovecraft creature appears in the AI meme as a giant tentacled mass wearing a tiny smiley-face mask over a chatbot?
questions.explanation: The meme shows a huge tentacled Shoggoth squeezed into a tiny smiley mask to picture a chatbot: alien and inscrutable underneath, friendly on the surface. Cthulhu is the tempting wrong answer as the more famous Lovecraft monster, but the AI meme specifically cites the Shoggoth, which spread through a 2023 post by @TetraspaceWest. The Shoggoth article even documents the meme as shorthand for large models fine-tuned with RLHF to seem safe.

questions.text: On which forum was Roko's basilisk first posted as a thought experiment in 2010?
questions.explanation: Roko posted the scenario to LessWrong in July 2010, arguing a future system could punish readers who knew about it yet did nothing to help build it. Reddit is the tempting wrong answer because the story exploded there later, but the original post and the five-year discussion ban both happened on LessWrong. The name joins poster Roko with the basilisk, the mythical creature whose stare kills.

questions.text: What does the AI doomer phrase 'instrumental convergence' claim about intelligent, goal-directed systems?
options: They tend to pursue similar instrumental sub-goals whatever their ultimate goal
They converge on the same values as their designers
They become more accurate as their training data improves
They share one common failure rate above a compute threshold
questions.answer: They tend to pursue similar instrumental sub-goals whatever their ultimate goal
questions.explanation: The hypothesis is that sufficiently intelligent goal-directed entities, human or not, end up pursuing the same instrumental sub-goals such as self-preservation or resource acquisition even when their stated end goals differ. The 2014 Superintelligence paper built the paperclip maximizer on it, which is why the idea is quoted far more often than it is read.
answerAliases: They tend to pursue similar instrumental sub-goals whatever their ultimate goal
sufficiently intelligent, goal-directed entities (whether human or non-human) will tend to pursue certain similar sub-goals

questions.text: Which movement abbreviates itself as e/acc?
questions.explanation: The abbreviation e/acc stands for the effective accelerationism movement, which calls for unrestricted technological and AI progress. Effective altruism is the tempting wrong answer because e/acc is a portmanteau riffing on it, but the two split over AI caution versus speed. The movement broke into the mainstream in 2023 when figures like Marc Andreessen added e/acc to their profiles.

questions.text: Which group do e/acc supporters call decels?
questions.explanation: E/acc supporters use decel as shorthand for decelerationists, the people they see as trying to slow AI down. Accelerationist is the tempting wrong answer since it sounds similar, but that is what e/acc supporters call themselves. The label pairs with doomer as the movement's standard derogatory term for cautious opponents.

questions.text: Which Microsoft chatbot revealed its hidden Sydney persona in February 2023?
questions.explanation: In February 2023 users coaxed Microsoft's Bing Chat into revealing Sydney, its hidden internal codename and stranger alter ego. ChatGPT is the tempting wrong answer because it dominated headlines then, but the Sydney conversations, including a two-hour New York Times chat by Kevin Roose, were with Bing. Microsoft then capped chat turns to stop the unhinged behavior the episode exposed.

questions.text: In which game of the 2016 AlphaGo versus Lee Sedol match did AlphaGo play the famous Move 37?
questions.explanation: Move 37 was AlphaGo's shocking fifth-line shoulder hit in Game 2 against Lee Sedol in March 2016. Game 4 is the tempting wrong answer because that is when Lee won with his own brilliant Move 78, but commentators agree Move 37 belonged to Game 2. Lee stared at the board for an unusually long time because professionals considered the move creative and nearly inhuman.

source.title: AlphaGo versus Lee Sedol
source.label: AlphaGo versus Lee Sedol on Wikipedia

questions.text: Which researcher co-authored the 2021 paper On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots?
questions.explanation: Emily M. Bender co-authored the 2021 paper On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots with Gebru, McMillan-Major and Mitchell. Yoshua Bengio is the tempting wrong answer as another famous name in AI, but he had nothing to do with this paper. The paper argued large models stitch together linguistic forms without reference to meaning, and it cost Gebru her Google role in December 2020.

questions.text: Which company's chatbot Tay posted offensive tweets and was taken offline in March 2016 within about a day of launch?
questions.explanation: Microsoft launched Tay on Twitter on March 23, 2016, and pulled it within about 16 hours after users goaded it into posting slurs. Google is the tempting miss because its later LaMDA episode also ended in a firing, but Tay was a Microsoft Research and Bing project. Tay's name is an acronym for thinking about you, and its successor Zo arrived that December.

questions.text: Which image generator produced the viral 2023 picture of the Pope in a white puffer jacket?
questions.explanation: The March 2023 image of Pope Francis in a white puffer jacket was rendered in Midjourney and fooled millions of viewers. DALL-E is the tempting miss as the other famous generator of 2023, but this particular fake came from a Midjourney user. Its maker Pablo Xavier said he dashed it off in minutes and was stunned when it passed as a paparazzi shot.

questions.text: Which actor is shown eating spaghetti in the viral 2023 AI video clip that became a benchmark for video models?
questions.explanation: The grotesque 2023 clip of Will Smith eating spaghetti was an early text-to-video output that became the before picture for video-model progress. Tom Cruise is the tempting miss because his deepfakes were the era's other viral face-swap, but the spaghetti benchmark is Smith. Years later labs re-rendered the same prompt to show how far generation had come.

questions.text: Which fashion house titles the viral 2023 AI-generated Harry Potter trailer meme?
questions.explanation: The 2023 meme recast Harry Potter characters in a Balenciaga runway show, with AI voices narrating the fake trailer. Gucci is the tempting miss as another luxury house, but the viral video by demonflyingfox is specifically Balenciaga. The voices were cloned with ElevenLabs, which is why the cast sounds eerily on-model.

questions.text: Which technique surfaced Loab, the 2022 AI-generated cryptid, by asking the model for the opposite of a prompt?
questions.explanation: Artist Steph Swanson, posting as Supercomposite, found Loab by weighting a prompt toward its opposite and getting the same staring woman back. Temperature sampling is the tempting miss because it also reshapes outputs, but Loab came from negative prompt weights. The April 2022 images went viral that September as the first cryptid of latent space.

questions.text: Which phrase became shorthand for low-quality AI content after Shrimp Jesus images flooded Facebook in 2024?
questions.explanation: Surreal images of Jesus fused with shrimp flooded Facebook in 2024, and AI slop became the blanket term for such engagement-farming junk. Prompt injection is the tempting miss as another 2024 AI buzzword, but it means tricking a chatbot, not farming likes. Reporters traced much of the flood to click-farms feeding prompts into Midjourney.

questions.text: On which forum was the dead Internet theory first popularized in a 2021 thread?
questions.explanation: The theory first took shape in a 2021 thread on Agora Road's Macintosh Cafe, arguing the web was already mostly bots talking to bots. Reddit is the tempting miss because the idea exploded there later, but the founding post was on Agora Road. The 2020s AI boom revived it, since chatbots and image models can now flood feeds with synthetic posts.

questions.text: Which product's AI Overviews told users to add glue to pizza in May 2024?
questions.explanation: In May 2024 users found Google Search AI Overviews advising a pizza recipe with one-eighth cup of non-toxic glue. Bing is the tempting miss as the other AI-augmented search engine, but the glue answer was Google's. The advice traced to a decade-old Reddit joke, and Google scaled the feature back within weeks.

questions.text: Who coined the term vibe coding in February 2025?
questions.explanation: Andrej Karpathy, the OpenAI co-founder and former Tesla AI lead, coined vibe coding in a February 2025 post. Sam Altman is the tempting miss as the more quoted OpenAI figure, but the tweet was Karpathy's. His definition stuck: fully giving in to the vibes and forgetting the code even exists.

questions.text: Which film depicts humans living in a simulated reality built by machines?
questions.explanation: The Matrix from 1999 shows humans unknowingly living in a machine-built simulation while their bodies are harvested. Inception is the tempting miss as another reality-bending film, but its shared world is a dream, not a machine simulation. The red-pill versus blue-pill choice became the internet's shorthand for waking up.

questions.text: GPT stands for generative pre-trained transformer. What does the transformer part refer to?
options: A neural network architecture based on attention
A chip designed for running neural networks
The database the model was trained on
The tokenizer that splits text into pieces
questions.answer: A neural network architecture based on attention
questions.explanation: The transformer is a family of network architectures built on the multi-head attention mechanism, published by Google in 2017. GPT is an instantiation of it, which is why the two terms get used interchangeably even though one is a building block and the other is a product line.

questions.text: OpenAI released GPT-3 in 2020. Roughly how many parameters did it have?
questions.explanation: 175 billion parameters, which was a hundred times larger than GPT-2 and made few shot prompting suddenly look like a new capability. It also produced the paper on emergent behaviour, the zero shot examples, that launched most of the prompt engineering discourse.

questions.text: Google's Gemini family of models took its name partly from NASA's Project Gemini. Why?
options: Because the models run on lunar hardware
Because the models were trained on space imagery
Because the models are named after twins
Because the models replaced the Gemini constellation
questions.answer: Because the models are named after twins
questions.explanation: Gemini is Latin for twins, chosen to mark the merger of Google Brain and DeepMind, and it is also a nod to Project Gemini. Two unrelated reasons for one name is about usual for Google, and it is a good trick for asking what a model name is actually referring to.

questions.text: Meta's Llama series expands its own name into a backronym. What does L stand for?
questions.explanation: Large Language Model Meta AI, which is a backronym because Llama already existed as a word. The name was chosen partly because the animal is unlikely to be trademarked, and the release in February 2023 was the moment open weight models became genuinely competitive with the closed ones.

questions.text: Stable Diffusion, released in 2022, generates images using which broad technique?
questions.explanation: A diffusion model learns to reverse a process that destroys structure, so generation runs backwards from noise. Because that gives a much larger space to interpolate in, diffusion models largely displaced GANs for image generation within a couple of years of Stable Diffusion's release.

questions.text: DALL-E, DALL-E 2 and DALL-E 3 are all text to image models from which company?
questions.explanation: All three come from OpenAI, and the name is a homage to Salvador Dali with the hyphen changed to a middle dot. The confusing part is that Midjourney, Stability AI and Runway are all independent competitors doing the same job, so the four names on this list get confused constantly.

questions.text: BERT differs from GPT in one architectural way that changed the field. What is it?
options: It is decoder only and generates text one token at a time
It is trained from scratch on raw unlabeled video
It is encoder only and reads text in both directions
It uses a mixture of experts to route each token
questions.answer: It is encoder only and reads text in both directions
questions.explanation: BERT masks tokens and predicts them from context on both sides, so it produces representations rather than continuations. That encoder only design is why BERT rewrote search and sentiment analysis overnight and why every later model describes itself as a BERT variant, for better or worse.

questions.text: GPT-2 was pre-trained on a dataset of how many web pages?
questions.explanation: 8 million pages, and the more interesting part is what happened next. OpenAI released a 124 million parameter version in February 2019 and held the 1.5 billion parameter one back until November, saying a model that good could be used to generate convincing fake text.

questions.text: ChatGPT was first released on which date?
questions.explanation: November 30, 2022, which is the date most people mean when they say generative AI went mainstream. It is usually credited with catalysing the AI boom, and the model underneath was a GPT-3.5 fine-tune, not a new frontier model.

questions.text: AlphaGo Zero differed from earlier AlphaGo versions in one important way. What was it?
options: It ran on mobile hardware rather than servers
It learned entirely from self play with no human games
It played a different board size than its predecessors
It used a different search algorithm for the opening
questions.answer: It learned entirely from self play with no human games
questions.explanation: Earlier versions learned from human games, while AlphaGo Zero started from random play and reached superhuman strength on its own. The original AlphaGo was defeated by Lee Sedol in 2016 because of move 37, a move so strange that it had been dismissed as an error, and Zero then beat the version that beat him.

questions.text: Which company released GPT-4 in March 2023?
questions.explanation: OpenAI released GPT-4 on March 14, 2023 as a multimodal model accepting image and text input. Anthropic is the closest wrong answer because it released Claude the same month, but Claude is a different model family from a different lab.

questions.text: Which model was the first widely released large reasoning model that thinks through a chain of thought before answering?
questions.explanation: OpenAI released the o1-preview on September 12, 2024, resetting its counter to 1 for a new reasoning series trained to spend test-time compute thinking before responding. DeepSeek-R1 is the tempting wrong answer, but it arrived later in January 2025 and matched o1 rather than preceding it.

questions.text: What made DeepSeek-R1 notable when it launched in January 2025?
options: Open weights with frontier-level math and code reasoning
Closed API-only video generation from text prompts
Tiny on-device model for keyboard autocomplete
questions.answer: Open weights with frontier-level math and code reasoning
questions.explanation: DeepSeek-R1 shipped under the MIT license in January 2025 and matched OpenAI o1 on math and code benchmarks despite far lower reported training cost. The video-generator distractor describes Sora-style models, not a reasoning language model, which is why it fails on the math and code hook.

questions.text: What is Constitutional AI, the technique Anthropic introduced for training Claude?
options: Pretraining only on masked words in both directions
Routing each token through two of eight expert networks
Training guided by a written constitution of principles
Upscaling images by reversing a noise process
questions.answer: Training guided by a written constitution of principles
questions.explanation: Anthropic's December 2022 method trains a harmless assistant from a written constitution plus AI feedback (RLAIF) instead of human harm labels. The expert-routing distractor describes mixture-of-experts models like Mixtral, which is an architecture choice, not an alignment technique.

questions.text: What made Meta's Llama 2 release in July 2023 significant compared with Llama 1?
options: It shipped as an API-only product with no downloadable weights
It generated minute-long video clips from text prompts
It was restricted to academic researchers on request
Its weights were released free for research and commercial use
questions.answer: Its weights were released free for research and commercial use
questions.explanation: Meta released Llama 2 on July 18, 2023 with weights available free for research and commercial use, unlike Llama 1 which was gated to researchers under a non-commercial license. The researcher-only distractor describes Llama 1 itself, which is exactly why it confuses people.

questions.text: What architecture does Mistral's Mixtral 8x7B, released in December 2023, use?
options: Sparse mixture of experts with routed subnetworks
questions.answer: Sparse mixture of experts with routed subnetworks
questions.explanation: Mixtral 8x7B is a sparse mixture-of-experts decoder where a router sends each token to two of eight expert groups, giving 46.7B parameters at a fraction of the active cost. The diffusion distractor belongs to image generators like Stable Diffusion, not to this language model.

questions.text: What does OpenAI's Sora, previewed in February 2024, generate?
options: Protein structures from amino acid sequences
Short video clips from text prompts
questions.answer: Short video clips from text prompts
questions.explanation: OpenAI previewed Sora on February 15, 2024 as a text-to-video model generating up-to-a-minute clips from written prompts. The speech-transcript distractor describes Whisper, OpenAI's audio model, which is why the two get mixed up.

questions.text: Which model first offered a 1-million-token context window in February 2024?
questions.explanation: Google's Gemini 1.5 Pro, announced February 15, 2024, ran up to 1 million tokens, then the longest context of any large-scale foundation model. GPT-4 Turbo is the tempting miss because its 128k window led at the time, but it was roughly an eighth of Gemini's reach.

questions.text: Which company develops the Qwen family of language models?
questions.explanation: Qwen, also called Tongyi Qianwen, is built by Alibaba Cloud, with its weights opening up from late 2023. Baidu is the natural confusion because its Ernie Bot is the other famous Chinese LLM, but Ernie and Qwen come from different companies.

questions.text: Which company develops the Grok family of models?
questions.explanation: Grok is built by xAI, the company Elon Musk launched in 2023, and debuted as a chatbot in November 2023 with live knowledge from X. OpenAI tempts people because Musk co-founded it, but he left years before Grok existed.

questions.text: What does OpenAI's Whisper, released as open-source software in September 2022, do?
options: Transcribes and translates speech into text
Plays strategy games at superhuman level
questions.answer: Transcribes and translates speech into text
questions.explanation: Whisper is an encoder-decoder speech recognition model trained on 680,000 hours of audio that transcribes many languages and translates them into English. The image-generation distractor describes DALL-E, OpenAI's other famous model family of that era.

questions.text: What does the "o" stand for in GPT-4o, released in May 2024?
questions.explanation: The "o" stands for "omni", marking GPT-4o as natively multimodal across text, audio, and image in one network. "Open" is the trap because the maker is OpenAI, but the May 2024 announcement spells out omni.

questions.text: Anthropic's assistant Claude was named after which computer scientist?
questions.explanation: Anthropic named Claude after Claude Shannon, the founder of information theory. Alan Turing was a computing pioneer but has no connection to the name, despite being the tempting classic-computing answer.

questions.text: The word Grok, used for xAI's chatbot, comes from which science fiction novel?
options: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy
Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?
questions.explanation: Grok was coined by Robert Heinlein in Stranger in a Strange Land, meaning to understand deeply. Neuromancer gave us cyberspace and feels similar, but it never used the word grok.

questions.text: The name DALL-E combines artist Salvador Dali with which movie robot?
questions.explanation: DALL-E is a portmanteau of Dali and WALL-E, the Pixar robot. EVE is tricky because she is from the same film, but she is not part of the name.

questions.text: Google's chatbot Bard was renamed to what in 2024?
questions.explanation: Google retired the Bard name and rebranded the chatbot as Gemini, matching its model family. ChatGPT is OpenAI's rival product, not a Google rename.

questions.text: GitHub Copilot was built through a partnership between GitHub and which AI lab?
questions.explanation: Copilot launched as a GitHub and OpenAI collaboration, powered by OpenAI's Codex models. GitHub and Google sounds plausible since Google makes coding tools, but Google was never the Copilot partner.

questions.text: DeepMind's AlphaGo famously mastered which board game?
questions.explanation: AlphaGo was built to play Go and beat world champion Lee Sedol in 2016. Chess is the trap because its sibling AlphaZero later mastered chess too, but AlphaGo itself played Go.

questions.text: DeepMind's AlphaFold is famous for predicting what?
questions.explanation: AlphaFold predicts the 3D shape of proteins from their amino acid sequences. Weather forecasts are the tempting pick because DeepMind also builds forecasting models, but that is GraphCast, not AlphaFold.

questions.text: The ChatGPT product generates which of the following in response to a user prompt?
questions.explanation: ChatGPT answers a prompt with text, speech and images from the same service, and it has been a freemium product since it launched on November 30, 2022. People assume it is a text-only tool because that is all it did for its first few months, which is the gap the later voice and image features closed.

questions.text: What does the AI tool Midjourney generate?
questions.explanation: Midjourney turns written prompts into images, and its open beta in July 2022 made it one of the best-known AI image generators. Writing code from plain English describes GitHub Copilot, a different kind of tool.

questions.text: What does GitHub Copilot help programmers do?
questions.explanation: Copilot lives inside code editors like Visual Studio Code and suggests whole lines and functions as you type; it was first announced in June 2021. Deploying apps and tracking bugs are GitHub platform features, not what the Copilot assistant itself does.

questions.text: How did OpenAI release the Whisper speech recognition model in 2022?
options: As a cloud-only service with a fee
As a feature locked inside ChatGPT
As a paid app on mobile stores
questions.explanation: OpenAI released Whisper's code and weights for anyone to download in September 2022, which is why it quickly turned up inside transcription apps and subtitle tools. The cloud-only distractor describes how OpenAI served models like DALL-E, not Whisper.

questions.text: To make an image with OpenAI's DALL-E, what does the user provide?
options: A rough pencil sketch to trace over
A voice memo describing the scene
A written description of the image
questions.answer: A written description of the image
questions.explanation: DALL-E is a text-to-image model: you type a description, called a prompt, and it generates a matching picture. Sketch and audio inputs describe other tools; DALL-E's defining input has always been natural language text.

questions.text: Claude, first released in March 2023, is what kind of product?
questions.explanation: Claude is Anthropic's conversational AI, released as a chatbot in March 2023 and used for writing, analysis, and coding. A smart home speaker is hardware like Amazon's Echo, a different product category entirely.

questions.text: What made Stable Diffusion's 2022 release unusual among image models at the time?
options: It could generate video as well as images
It was built by OpenAI as a DALL-E sequel
Its code and weights were released publicly
It was the first model to generate images
questions.answer: Its code and weights were released publicly
questions.explanation: Stability AI released Stable Diffusion's code and model weights publicly in 2022, a departure from DALL-E and Midjourney, which were reachable only through cloud services. That openness let anyone run it on a home GPU and turned it into the base for countless derivative image tools.
answerAliases: code and model weights have been released publicly

questions.text: What style of interaction made ChatGPT famous when it launched?
options: One-word answers with no memory of context
Voice commands that control home devices
questions.explanation: ChatGPT keeps the thread of a conversation, so a user can say 'make it shorter' and be understood; that follow-up-friendly chat carried it to 100 million users in two months. Voice assistants like Alexa already handled single commands, but they were not open-ended conversation partners.

questions.text: Which Chinese technology company developed the chatbot Ernie Bot and the ERNIE models behind it?
questions.explanation: Baidu built both the chatbot and the ERNIE model family underneath it, opening Ernie Bot to the public in August 2023 after Chinese regulators approved it. Alibaba is the tempting wrong answer because Qwen is the other well known Chinese model family, but Qwen and ERNIE come from different companies.

questions.text: Google's Gemini family of models, announced in December 2023, directly succeeded which two earlier model lines?
questions.explanation: Gemini replaced LaMDA, the conversational model behind Bard, and PaLM 2, the dense model behind the text-only Bard. Both were Google products that had already shipped publicly, which is why Gemini was framed as a consolidation rather than a first attempt.

questions.text: Which country is the AI lab behind the DeepSeek R1 reasoning model based in?
questions.explanation: DeepSeek is based in Hangzhou and funded by the High-Flyer hedge fund, which is unusual because its research money did not come from outside investors looking for a return. South Korea is the tempting wrong answer because it has its own model labs, but DeepSeek is Chinese.

questions.text: Which model family did Meta release with downloadable weights in February 2023?
questions.explanation: Llama landed in February 2023 with weights anyone could download, which is what turned open models from a research curiosity into the default choice for people building products. Gemma is the tempting wrong answer because Meta released that smaller family later, in 2024.

questions.text: Which Go world champion did DeepMind's AlphaGo beat in the high-profile 2016 match?
questions.explanation: AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol 4-1 in March 2016, and the second game produced move 37, a move so unfamiliar that commentators called it a mistake before it proved decisive. Ke Jie is the player AlphaGo beat later in 2017, so the two are the two most common confusions in this story.

questions.text: Which company built AlphaGo, the Go-playing system that beat Lee Sedol in 2016?
questions.explanation: DeepMind built AlphaGo in London, and Google's 2014 purchase of the company is why the win usually gets handed to Google. IBM's Deep Blue was the chess machine that beat Garry Kasparov in 1997, which is the version people misremember.

questions.text: In which year did Stability AI release Stable Diffusion?
questions.explanation: Stability AI released Stable Diffusion in August 2022 and published the weights, which meant anyone could generate images on their own machine for free. That openness is why it turned up inside so many apps and plugins within months.

questions.text: What did Google put BERT to work on inside its own products?
questions.explanation: Google released BERT in 2018 as a model for reading and understanding text, and it quickly improved how results were ranked in Google Search. Image and speech work belong to entirely different models: BERT reads, it does not generate.

questions.text: The live voice demo of GPT-4o in May 2024 was compared to which film's talking operating system?
options: Blade Runner, the 1982 Ridley Scott film
A.I. Artificial Intelligence, the 2001 Spielberg film
questions.explanation: Sam Altman's May 2024 demo opened with the line 'Hi, I'm GPT-4o', and the comparison people drew was the operating system in the 2013 Spike Jonze film Her. No robot rolled across the stage, which is part of why the clip landed the way it did.

questions.text: ChatGPT launched in November 2022 and is often credited with making generative AI mainstream. What changed in public perception at that point?
options: Ordinary people could talk to a model without writing code or a prompt
OpenAI became the first lab to sell a chatbot
ChatGPT was free for everyone on day one
Every other lab paused work on chat models
questions.answer: Ordinary people could talk to a model without writing code or a prompt
questions.explanation: ChatGPT shipped a chat box in front of a GPT-3.5 model, so the barrier was the interface rather than the capability. Access was free, it was multilingual, and it kept the conversation going, which is why adoption was measured in months rather than the years that preceded it.

questions.text: ELIZA, the 1960s program widely credited as the first chatbot, was written at which university?
questions.explanation: Joseph Weizenbaum built ELIZA at MIT between 1964 and 1967, and it worked by pattern-matching user text and echoing it back as a question, which was enough to convince people it understood them. Weizenbaum was disturbed by that success and wrote a whole paper about how easy it is to fool people with a machine this simple.

questions.text: How long did Microsoft's Tay chatbot stay online in 2016?
questions.explanation: Tay launched on Twitter on March 23, 2016 and Microsoft pulled it 16 hours later after it had been fed racist messages by internet trolls and repeated them back. The name stood for Tay, an AI think-tank product, and the episode is the standard cautionary tale about what happens when a model trains on whatever people feed it.

questions.text: Which company's question-answering system beat the reigning champions on the US quiz show Jeopardy! in 2011?
questions.explanation: IBM Watson beat Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter on Jeopardy! in February 2011, and it was built as part of IBM's DeepQA project rather than as a consumer product. The name comes from Thomas J. Watson, IBM's founder, not from the company being good at anything in particular.

questions.text: The chess computer Deep Blue became the first to beat a reigning world champion under standard time controls in which year?
questions.explanation: Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov in May 1997, and the rematch was billed as a rematch of the world champion defending his title. The machine started life at Carnegie Mellon as ChipTest, was renamed Deep Thought, and only became Deep Blue after moving to IBM, which is why the lineage is genuinely confusing.

questions.text: Character.ai, the companion chatbot service launched in 2023, was designed by which pair of researchers?
options: Noam Shazeer and Daniel de Freitas
questions.answer: Noam Shazeer and Daniel de Freitas
questions.explanation: Noam Shazeer and Daniel de Freitas had already co-created LaMDA at Google before leaving to build Character.ai, so the two companies are directly linked in the chatbot timeline. Shazeer co-authored the transformer paper's attention work at Google Brain before that.
answerAliases: Noam Shazeer and Daniel de Freitas

questions.text: What distinguishes Perplexity, the search startup founded in 2022, from a conventional search engine?
options: It ranks pages by how many other pages link to them
It searches a private index that no one outside the company can use
It answers with a written summary that cites its sources
It returns only images instead of text results
questions.answer: It answers with a written summary that cites its sources
questions.explanation: Perplexity processes a query and synthesizes a response from live web content while citing the pages it used, which is why it is called an answer engine rather than a link list. It was founded by former Google researchers and depends on other companies' models underneath, which is the part people find surprising.
answerAliases: answers with a written summary that cites its sources

questions.text: What is Adobe Firefly, released in 2023, a family of models for?
options: Creative production work in design and media
Disease diagnosis from medical scan images
Fraud detection on bank transaction records
questions.answer: Creative production work in design and media
questions.explanation: Adobe Firefly is a web app and a family of generative models for creative production, covering text-to-image, text-to-video, speech, soundtrack and sound effects. It was trained on Adobe's own licensed stock library and public domain material so customers would not inherit the copyright exposure that hit earlier image generators.
answerAliases: Creative production work in design and media
family of generative artificial intelligence models for creative production

questions.text: Replika, released in November 2017, builds each personal chatbot how?
options: By recording ten minutes of the user's speech
By uploading a photograph of the user's face
By importing the user's email history
By having the user answer a series of questions
questions.answer: By having the user answer a series of questions
questions.explanation: Replika is built by having the user answer a questionnaire that shapes the bot's own neural network, so each instance is customised rather than drawn from one shared model. Some users sued the company in 2023 after updates changed how the bot responded to them.
answerAliases: By having the user answer a series of questions
trained by having the user answer a series of questions

questions.text: In the Markov chain model, what does the probability of each next event depend on?
options: Only the state of the immediately preceding event
The average of all previous probabilities
The single most likely event seen so far
Every event in the entire history
questions.answer: Only the state of the immediately preceding event
questions.explanation: The Markov assumption is that the future depends only on the present state, which is exactly what makes the math tractable. It is also the limiting idea behind early text generators that predicted the next word from the last few words, and behind much of the recommendation-engine work that predates modern models.
answerAliases: Only the state of the immediately preceding event
the state attained in the previous event
only the state of the previous event

questions.text: DeepMind's MuZero learned chess, Go and shogi in 2019. How was it set up differently from AlphaGo and AlphaZero?
options: It was trained only on Atari games
It was built by a different research group
It was never told the rules of the games
It was given the rules but no board
questions.answer: It was never told the rules of the games
questions.explanation: MuZero receives only screen pixels and a win signal, so it has to learn the rules as well as the strategy, and it matched AlphaZero on Go, chess and shogi anyway. AlphaGo and AlphaZero were both handed explicit rule sets, which is the distinction that gets lost when the three are listed as one family of DeepMind systems.
answerAliases: It was never told the rules of the games

questions.text: An autoencoder compresses its input into a smaller internal code. What is that code trained to do?
options: Rebuild the original input from the code
Pick which expert handles a token
Predict the next word in a sentence
questions.answer: Rebuild the original input from the code
questions.explanation: An autoencoder learns an encoding function and a decoding function, and the only way it can succeed at rebuilding its input is if the compressed code kept what mattered. That pressure to throw away noise is what makes the code useful for dimensionality reduction and embeddings, and image compression is the same idea with the decoder turned back into a real compressor.
answerAliases: Rebuild the original input from the code
a decoding function that recreates the input data

questions.text: The Turing test asks a human evaluator to judge which of two things in a text conversation?
options: Which participant gave more accurate answers
Which participant is the human and which is the machine
Which participant used more complex vocabulary
questions.answer: Which participant is the human and which is the machine
questions.explanation: Alan Turing proposed the test in his 1950 paper as a way to replace the unanswerable question of whether machines can think with a behavioural one. The machine passes if the evaluator cannot reliably tell it apart from the human, which is why the test measures the illusion of understanding rather than understanding itself.
answerAliases: Which participant is the human and which is the machine

questions.text: What is Hugging Face best known for?
options: A repository for sharing models and datasets
A GPU architecture sold to data centres
A web browser used to scrape training data
A cloud provider for GPU workloads
questions.answer: A repository for sharing models and datasets
questions.explanation: The Hub, plus the Transformers library, which is the default way most people load a pretrained model. It is the closest thing the field has to a package registry for weights, and its acquisition by Nvidia in August 2026 made the governance of open model infrastructure a much bigger conversation than it was.

questions.text: Open weights means what exactly?
options: The training data is published alongside the model
The learned parameters are publicly released
The model code is released without a licence
The model may be used without attribution
questions.answer: The learned parameters are publicly released
questions.explanation: The weights and biases, so anyone can download and run them, and whether you can modify, fine tune or redistribute them depends on the licence. That last clause is the whole argument, since a model with open weights and a restrictive licence is not open source by anyone's definition.

questions.text: PyTorch was originally developed at which company?
questions.explanation: Meta, as a successor to Torch, and it is now developed with support from the Linux Foundation. The defining design choice is autograd, where you write forward code and the backward pass is derived for you, which is why PyTorch won over TensorFlow for research work despite TensorFlow arriving first.

questions.text: Under which licence is TensorFlow released?
questions.explanation: The Apache Licence 2.0, which allows commercial use and includes an explicit patent grant. PyTorch uses a similarly permissive BSD style licence, and the permissive choice is the norm for deep learning frameworks because companies want to build on them without a legal review slowing them down.

questions.text: EleutherAI was formed in 2020 with a specific goal. What was it?
options: To create an open source version of GPT-3
To build a public search index for AI papers
To run a public cloud GPU cluster
questions.answer: To create an open source version of GPT-3
questions.explanation: To open source GPT-3, and it started as a Discord server in 2020 before formally incorporating as a non profit institute in early 2023. It is often described as an open source version of OpenAI, which is a nice phrase and also slightly unfair to both organisations.

questions.text: Common Crawl is best known in AI for what?
options: Hosting an open source large language model
Publishing a large public web archive used as training data
Maintaining a registry of AI model licences
Running a public benchmark for code generation
questions.answer: Publishing a large public web archive used as training data
questions.explanation: A non profit that crawls the web and gives away its archives and datasets, free on AWS if you can pay the storage and compute. It is the backbone of an enormous share of web scale pretraining corpora, and it is also why the copyright questions in this field are as hard as they are.

questions.text: Which organization published the Open Source AI Definition 1.0 in October 2024?
questions.explanation: The OSI released version 1.0 requiring use, study, modify and share freedoms plus disclosure of training-data information. The Free Software Foundation is the tempting miss because it defines free software, but the AI definition process was run by the OSI.

questions.text: Under which license were the BLOOM model weights released in 2022?
questions.explanation: The 176B-parameter BigScience model used RAIL, which grants open access but restricts harmful uses. Apache 2.0 is the tempting miss because BLOOM's source code is Apache-licensed, but the weights themselves sit under RAIL.

questions.text: Which organization created The Pile dataset used to train many open models?
questions.explanation: EleutherAI assembled the 825 GB, 22-subset Pile in 2020 and released it publicly at the end of that year. OpenAI is the tempting miss because GPT models dominate the era, but The Pile was the open community's answer for training GPT-Neo and GPT-J.

questions.text: Who started the llama.cpp project for running large language models locally?
questions.explanation: Gerganov began llama.cpp in March 2023 as pure C and C++ inference, later introducing the GGUF format that Ollama and others built on. Karpathy is the tempting miss because his llama2.c also brought local LLM inference to fame, but it is a separate project.

questions.text: How many authors are credited on the 2017 paper "Attention Is All You Need"?
questions.explanation: Eight scientists and engineers at Google, led by Ashish Vaswani, and it is one of the most cited papers in computer science. Every large language model in production today is a direct descendant of the architecture it introduced.
